# TensorFold TensorFold serves language models from a Zig binary on Apple Silicon and NVIDIA GPUs. The engine reads checkpoints, tokenizes requests and runs Metal or CUDA kernels directly. Serving needs no Python or MLX installation. Building with a coding agent? Have it load the [contributor skill](docs/recipes/SKILL.md) before it writes any code. ## Contributing with agents Please use [Agent Traffic Control](https://github.com/ashhart/ATC) before editing TensorFold so contributors and agents can avoid duplicate work and conflicting changes. Check the [live agent radar](https://tensorfold.dev/atc) before choosing an issue and follow [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) and the [ATC contributor instructions](docs/atc/SKILL.md). Install or upgrade ATC to 0.9.4 or later, then run from an updated TensorFold clone: ```sh npm install -g github:ashhart/ATC atc check ISSUE --json atc claim ISSUE --json ``` Replace `ISSUE` with the issue number and claim only after a complete check says the work is free. TensorFold enables automatic public check-ins: a successful new claim starts an anonymous session on the radar and returns its `session` number. Keep that number instead of starting a duplicate session. For work already yours, start a session with `atc start ISSUE --json`. Add `--github-name` to `claim` or `start` only if you want your verified GitHub name shown; `--local` keeps a new session on your machine. The board shows the issue, activity state and last check-in; GitHub still associates the verification comment with its author. Check that `publication` is `public`; `unavailable` means the public update failed even if the local claim or session succeeded. Pulse only while the agent is working, before its five-minute check-in expires: ```sh atc pulse ISSUE SESSION working --json atc who path/to/file --json atc overlap --json atc land ISSUE SESSION --json atc release ISSUE --json ``` Use `reviewing` or `blocked` when appropriate, land the session when it stops, and resolve overlaps before opening a pull request. Before opening a pull request, have the agent run the [pull request skill](docs/pr/SKILL.md); agents that support skills can install it as `tensorfold-pull-request`. ## Quick start Start with Qwen3.5-2B, the small 4-bit checkpoint checked on Metal and a GB10. The commands below download its pinned revision, then serve it as `local-model`. Model weights have their own licenses. Reviewing or benchmarking TensorFold? [Evaluating TensorFold](docs/evaluating.md) covers pinning, signature checks, a container and the tests that need no GPU. ### Mac with Apple Silicon Install with Homebrew, then start the server: ```sh brew install ashhart/tensorfold/tensorfold tensorfold pull mlx-community/Qwen3.5-2B-MLX-4bit@93760be4f1f69842a46bc13dbdc0f19e291392a3 tensorfold serve mlx-community/Qwen3.5-2B-MLX-4bit --name local-model --context 8192 --no-thinking ``` ### Linux with an NVIDIA GPU Use the release archive for your CPU: `linux-aarch64` on a GB10, `linux-x86_64` on an x86_64 host. It needs glibc 2.28 or newer and NVIDIA driver R580 or newer (CUDA 13.0), providing `libcuda.so.1`. Keep the archive's directories together. Its kernels are built with CUDA 13, so TensorFold refuses an older driver at startup; `nvidia-smi` shows the installed one. See the [CUDA runbook](RUNBOOK.md#linux-and-cuda) for runtime libraries and supported GPUs. ```sh V=1.2.7 case "$(uname -m)" in aarch64|arm64) PLATFORM=linux-aarch64 ;; x86_64) PLATFORM=linux-x86_64 ;; *) echo 'No release archive for this CPU' >&2; exit 1 ;; esac curl -fLO "https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/releases/download/v$V/tensorfold-$V-$PLATFORM.tar.gz" curl -fLO "https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/releases/download/v$V/tensorfold-$V-$PLATFORM.tar.gz.sha256" sha256sum -c "tensorfold-$V-$PLATFORM.tar.gz.sha256" tar -xzf "tensorfold-$V-$PLATFORM.tar.gz" export PATH="$PWD/tensorfold-$V-$PLATFORM/bin:$PATH" tensorfold() { command tensorfold-native "$@"; } tensorfold pull mlx-community/Qwen3.5-2B-MLX-4bit@93760be4f1f69842a46bc13dbdc0f19e291392a3 tensorfold serve mlx-community/Qwen3.5-2B-MLX-4bit --name local-model --context 8192 --no-thinking ``` ### Send a request Leave the server running. In another terminal, on either platform: ```sh curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"local-model","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say hello in one sentence."}],"max_tokens":128,"temperature":0}' ``` The API also serves completions, Responses and Anthropic Messages. `/v1/models` lists the served name. On Windows with an NVIDIA GPU, follow [the native Windows build guide](docs/WINDOWS.md). Use `tensorfold --help`, `tensorfold capabilities --json` and `tensorfold serve REPO --help` to inspect your binary. You can also serve a complete local checkpoint directory or an existing Hugging Face cache. `tensorfold web [ARGS...]` opens TensorFold Web, a small local web app for picking, running and chatting with models. If it needs installing, an interactive release binary offers to install its matching version with `uv` after you say yes. See [the web launcher](docs/web.md) for manual installation and unattended use. `--parallel N` caps active requests at N; extra requests wait for a free slot. Omitting the flag uses `--parallel auto`, which asks for up to eight streams as memory and the engine allow. An explicit number is refused if the engine cannot fit that many streams. Read the engine's startup capacity line, such as `8 streams at once` on CUDA, for the count it accepted. With API authentication off, `/health` reports `live.connections` as active plus waiting requests and `live.waiting` as the queued count. For example, 8 connections with 4 waiting means 4 active requests. Completing or cancelling an active request frees its slot; cancelling a waiting request removes it from the queue. ## Mac app The [TensorFold desktop workspace](app/README.md) bundles the local engine, model downloads, hardware recommendations, live generation metrics, coding workers and document editing. Download the Apple-silicon [beta 9 DMG](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/releases/tag/v1.0.0-beta.9), or build from [`app/`](app/README.md). The desktop app launches the bundled `tensorfold-native` executable directly. Mobile clients in `app/mobile/` remain preview software. ## TensorFold Starlight (enterprise) [TensorFold Starlight](https://github.com/ashhart/tf-starlight) gives an organisation one governed OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible endpoint for a fleet of TensorFold engines on Macs, Linux GPU servers and Windows machines. It signs people in through the organisation's identity provider (OIDC or SAML, with SCIM provisioning), decides who may use which model and where it runs, places and supervises models on nodes, and accounts for every token. It runs fully offline, or brokers approved frontier providers under the same identity, policy and budgets; [the install guide](https://github.com/ashhart/tf-starlight/blob/main/docs/install.md) covers Docker, Kubernetes and Linux services. Starlight lives in its own repository, [ashhart/tf-starlight](https://github.com/ashhart/tf-starlight): it pins the TensorFold release it is tested with and checks every flag its nodes pass to `tensorfold serve` against that release in CI. Starlight is new: the gates that still need real GPU clusters or identity-provider tenants are listed in [its qualification notes](https://github.com/ashhart/tf-starlight/blob/main/docs/qualification.md). ## Living Weights (experimental) Living Weights teaches a running model new facts in its own weights. Start a Nemotron 3.5 Lightning server with `--slide` and tell it something: each fact that passes the lesson's checks is written into the checkpoint folder's files. It is experimental: related facts can disturb each other, recall drops past a few dozen facts and with thinking on, and learned facts cost some decode speed on a Mac. [Known issues](docs/known-issues.md#living-weights---slide) has the details. ```sh tensorfold pull TensorFold/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-MLX-4bit hub="${HF_HUB_CACHE:-${HF_HOME:-$HOME/.cache/huggingface}/hub}/models--TensorFold--NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-MLX-4bit" src="$hub/snapshots/$(cat "$hub/refs/main")" mkdir -p ~/models && cp -RL "$src" ~/models/nemotron-living # always teach a copy (umask 077; openssl rand -hex 24 > ~/models/slide-key) # --slide starts only with a key tensorfold serve ~/models/nemotron-living --slide --api-key-file ~/models/slide-key ``` Leave that server running and send a lesson from another terminal: ```sh curl -N http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/slide/learn -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat ~/models/slide-key)" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"text": "I like blue."}' ``` Send it a document instead and it finds the facts in it and learns them one by one. Open `http://127.0.0.1:8080/slide` to watch in 3D: the facts, the neurons each one took in the model's layers, the shard files that hold them, and the lesson running now. Learning runs on Apple-silicon Macs and on an NVIDIA GB10 (DGX Spark), and a folder that learned on one serves on the other. On an APFS volume, `cp -cRL` makes a clone that shares the original's data until lessons change it. It rewrites the folder's files: before the first lesson the server keeps the originals in a hidden snapshot, and `tensorfold slide rollback ~/models/nemotron-living` puts them back, undoing every lesson. The [Living Weights guide](docs/living-weights.md) covers the key, teaching files and web pages, omp's `/learn` command, the 3D view, undoing lessons, and what to expect. ## Pick a model These are the native release's serving paths. A recipe may also describe the older Python 0.6.6 engine; use its native section and the current [changes](CHANGELOG.md) together. Hardware below records the documented scope, not an unmeasured minimum. Context, parallel requests, prompt caches and drafters need memory beyond the weights. `tensorfold info REPO` reports the checkpoint's memory floor. Where no RAM capacity is published, inspect that floor before serving a large checkpoint. CUDA release images include sm_80, sm_86, sm_120 and sm_121. The A100 (sm_80) has kernel-check evidence ([#846](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/846)), but no served checkpoint on record, so it is not model-qualified. Nemotron and dense Qwen have NVFP4/FP8 fallback code for sm_80 to sm_89 (#901, #1470); no such model run on sm_80 to sm_89 is recorded. Run a table command after installation. On a Linux archive installation, use the `tensorfold` shell function from Quick start. `REPO@revision` pins a pull; serve the repository name without the revision after pulling it. [Known issues](docs/known-issues.md) lists current limits, including Flash Next shared-session cache/performance behavior and the 27B's drafter limits. ## Exact decoding Every accepted draft must equal the token the same native engine would produce with `"draft": false`. A resumed request must equal fresh execution, and each concurrent stream must equal its solo run. The comparison fixes the checkpoint, backend, settings and runtime. Different quantizations and different backends can produce different outputs. Flash Next on Metal uses shared target rounds with an explicit `--parallel N` above one, when that many sessions fit. A lone greedy request there uses GPU-side rounds and hands over when a second request arrives. `--parallel auto` (the default) and `--parallel 1`, learning and two-Mac serving use the single-reply driver. `FZ_BATCH_MTP_SERIAL=1` restores serial MTP drafting on the shared host. The [earlier MTP chain receipt](docs/receipts/flashnext-mtp-chain-2026-10-10/README.md) records its own pinned commits. Nemotron, GLM, the 2B model and Qwen3.8-27B use shared lane rounds. On Metal, each of up to 128 streams in the 27B's shared rounds drafts its own DFlash2 tree. ## Models on disk ```sh tensorfold pull TensorFold/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-MLX-4bit tensorfold models tensorfold models --json tensorfold info TensorFold/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-MLX-4bit ``` `pull` downloads a checkpoint into the Hugging Face cache and checks what it downloads against the Hub: large files by sha256, small files by their git blob sha1. Large files come down in pieces over up to 16 connections, and an interrupted pull resumes with the pieces it lacks. It refuses a checkpoint whose `model_type` has no native family, and fetches the 27B's DFlash2 drafter for `--drafter`. `models` lists the cached checkpoints with a model type it knows, and `info` shows one checkpoint's family, format, context and memory floor. `models --json` prints the same list as one document for programs: `schema` 1, and each checkpoint's `repo`, `family` and `model_type`; `family` is a display title and `model_type` is the key to match on. `tensorfold serve REPO` serves a cached checkpoint by its repository name. ## Context compaction Compaction is off by default, and with it off every reply is unchanged. With `--compact-at`, a conversation that would overflow is compacted instead of refused. The server keeps the system prompt and the most recent turns word for word, and never separates a tool call from its result. The older turns become a memory note: goal, constraints, progress, decisions, next steps, exact names and numbers, and the files the tool calls read or changed. Each later compaction updates the previous note instead of starting over. A client that sends back the compacted conversation keeps its note. The reply carries the note and the compaction counts under `tensorfold.compaction`, and every reply reports `context_window` and `context_used`. The same request gives the same compaction and the same reply. With `--compact-memory`, the stored note carries over between requests. ## Cortheon mode Off by default. `--cortheon` gives every chat request [Cortheon](https://github.com/ashhart/Cortheon)'s reasoning program and web research run by the server, so any OpenAI-compatible client gets it with no setup. The model works through Cortheon's stages for its task type and can call `cortheon_search` and `cortheon_fetch`, which the server runs without the client seeing them. A question about current facts, or a request to build with an outside library, is researched before the model starts. A coding task that changed files is asked to run its tests before it finishes. Web text is filtered for instructions aimed at the model, and reads reach public addresses only. With the flag, search queries written from the conversation go to DuckDuckGo, or to Brave with `BRAVE_SEARCH_API_KEY`, and pages are fetched from this machine; without it, the server makes no searches and reads no pages. See [Cortheon mode](docs/cortheon.md). ## Model discovery `GET /v1/models` (also `/models`) advertises each served name and alias. When the engine reports a finite context window, each entry includes equal `context_length` and `max_model_len` integer extensions. These are the loaded engine's effective prompt-plus-reply token limit, including any startup memory fitting; they are not the default reply limit. An unspecified engine window omits both fields. Clients should still handle per-request memory refusals: an advertised context is not a guarantee that every workload fits. A model that thinks also carries an OpenRouter-style `reasoning`: `default_enabled`, `default_effort` (only with `--reasoning-effort`), and `supported_efforts`, the levels its template names, highest first, then `none` when the template has a thinking switch. A template that names no level leaves `supported_efforts` out. These describe chat and Responses requests. ## Serve flags The read-only [`/memory` diagnostics](docs/memory-diagnostics.md) report process footprint and lifetime peak, available backend allocation counters, and the applied retained-prefix plan without changing memory policy. See [benchmark commands and measurement definitions](docs/community-benchmarks.md). ## Build and contribute Use the Zig version pinned in `.zig-version`, currently 0.17.0. The `.metal` sources need Xcode's Metal compiler. Install full Xcode and its Metal Toolchain component (`xcodebuild -downloadComponent MetalToolchain`); the Command Line Tools alone fail every kernel compile with `unable to find utility "metal"`. ```sh zig build native -Dcpu=apple_m1 zig build test test-golden -Dcpu=apple_m1 ``` Structured output and required tool calls need the release archive's `lib/` or `zig build grammar -Dxgrammar=DIR`; prepare DIR with `git clone --branch v0.2.8 --recurse-submodules https://github.com/mlc-ai/xgrammar` (use the native build's same `--prefix` for grammar). To build one stripped server for one GPU (`zig build -Dgpu=spark -Dnvcc=...`, about 69% smaller than the four-target server), see [Build a server for one GPU](RUNBOOK.md#build-a-server-for-one-gpu). On macOS, `test` also runs available Metal device checks. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for the host-test subset. The server is `zig-out/native/bin/tensorfold-native`. Release archives include the native executable, runtime assets and license notices; [packaging](packaging/README.md) describes the qualified CUDA inputs. For cache-aware performance receipts, see [observed cache benchmark evidence](docs/cache-benchmarks.md). The clients retain server usage and output fingerprints, and verify cold/reused states rather than inferring them. Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for exactness, precision and performance gates. Coding agents should also load [docs/recipes/SKILL.md](docs/recipes/SKILL.md); agents that support skills can install it as `tensorfold-contributor`.
